newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian eunuchs seek sympathy through book.
newsitem.headline: Indian eunuchs seek sympathy through book.

text.p: Indian eunuchs, known as Hijras, surprised officegoers in Bombay's crowded business district on Friday by offering for sale a book written about themselves.
Onlookers thronged the city's Flora Fountain plaza, where the Hijras, dressed like women in silk saris, displayed for sale the 32-page booklet "Hijras: Who We Are".
Professionally designed and published in English, the book, an account of Meena Balaji, a Hijra, as told to Canadian author Ruth Lor Malloy, has been well-received.
"Give Hijras a chance," urged a huge billboard on a building near the plaza. "Read 'Hijras: Who We Are'," it said.
A policeman advised the Hijras to move on and sell the book elsewhere as a huge crowd gathered, causing a traffic jam.
Balaji, a stocky eunuch dressed in a dark blue silk sari with his face heavily made up, led a team of Hijras, all dressed as women, carrying bundles of the books.
"It's the point of view of a Hijra aimed at changing people's attitudes towards these hapless people," Meenakshi Shah, a social worker associated with the book, told Reuters.
Hijras, a common sight in Indian cities, often have to eke out a living by begging or offering themselves as prostitutes.
"We are people too. In the world of men and women we are neither. Because we are different, everyone shuns us," Meena is quoted in the book as saying.
"We all prefer dressing up in women's clothes, wearing jewellery and make-up, because we feel we are women. We take female names and keep our hair long," Meena added.
The Hijras have a community of their own, complete with elaborate rituals and a goddess to worship.
The book gives a description of the ritual castration that converts a man into a Hijra.
"Please, understand that castration is very important for us. We have an operation for religious reasons, and to become more like a woman," said Meena in the book.
Meena denied that any young boys had been kidnapped by other Hijras and forcibly castrated.
"How is such a thing possible? It is not true at all," he said.
The book does not give estimates of the number of Hijras in Bombay or in other parts of the country.
"We were born like we are. We can't help it. Why do people shun us or are scared of us?" asked Meena.
